For the water process engineer, the power of ML is unlocked by framing operational challenges as specific, answerable questions. The type of question asked determines the type of ML task employed. In the context of a WRRF, these tasks can be grouped into a few key categories, each with direct Integration of Data Driven Process Control for Maximizing Energy and Resource Efficiency in WRRFs 9 relevance to improving process control and efficiency. This section reframes abstract ML concepts into the practical language of water process engineering, using the case studies from this report as concrete examples of data-driven problem-solving in action. 2.2.1 Prediction (Regression): Answering "How Much?" or "What Will the Value Be?" Perhaps the most common and intuitive application of ML in water process engineering is regression, the task of predicting a specific, continuous numerical value (Seborg et al. 2011). Regression models answer questions like "how much?" or "what will the value be at a future time?" This capability is fundamental to proactive control, allowing engineers to anticipate system states and make adjustments before deviations occur. The case studies in this report provide several powerful examples of regression in practice. • Optimizing Phosphorus Recovery (Application 4): To improve the efficiency of the MagPrex® system, an ML model was developed to predict daily influent orthophosphate (OP) concentrations. This forecast provides operators with timely guidance to adjust magnesium chloride (MgCl) dosing, moving beyond a reliance on infrequent weekly lab samples and preventing costly chemical overdosing. • Controlling Biosolids Concentration (Application 5): In the holistic biosolids optimization study, an ML model was trained to forecast total solids (TS) percentages using data from a non-contact acoustic sensor. This real-time prediction is designed to inform automated adjustments to dilution water, ensuring stable feed concentrations for downstream processes like thermal hydrolysis and digestion. • Enhancing Disinfection Efficacy (Application 3): For PAA disinfection, a key challenge is determining the correct dose under varying conditions. A regression model was developed to estimate the required integrated concentration x time (iCT), a critical parameter that dictates disinfection performance. By predicting the necessary iCT based on real-time water quality, the system can move towards more precise and cost-effective dosing strategies. 2.2.2 Classification: Answering "Which Category?" or "Is this Condition A or B?" A second key task is classification, which involves assigning a discrete, categorical label to an observation (Seborg et al. 2011). Rather than predicting a precise number, a classifier answers a question like, "Is this condition A or B?" or "Which operational state are we in?" Classification can often provide a more direct and actionable insight for operators. The P-recovery case study (Application 4) offers a compelling example of how reframing a problem from regression to classification can unlock greater operational value.
